tanska-hoffman-klementyna.name: Tanska Hoffman, Klementyna
tanska-hoffman-klementyna.bio: Klementyna Tanska Hoffmanowa (1798-1845) was a Polish writer and educator, among the first women in Poland to earn her living by the pen. Born in Warsaw, she wrote widely for young readers and on the moral education of women; The Journal of Countess Francoise Krasinska (1825), an imagined diary of an eighteenth-century Polish noblewoman, is her best-known work and an early example of the historical-diary novel.

books.title: The Journal of Countess Francoise Krasinska

rychlowska-marianna.name: Rychlowska, Marianna
rychlowska-marianna.bio: Marianna Rychlowska wrote the introductions to two Polish titles issued by Skomlin Press: Klementyna Tanska Hoffmanowa's The Journal of Countess Francoise Krasinska and Wladyslaw Stanislaw Reymont's The Comedienne, the latter reprinting Edmund Obecny's 1920 translation. Her introduction to The Comedienne sets out Reymont's life, the historical setting of the novel, and the early history of the Polish theatre, supplying context the original audience would have taken for granted.

books.title: The Journal of Countess Francoise Krasinska

stein-alex.name: Stein, Alex
stein-alex.bio: Alex Stein is an American essayist, aphorist and illustrator. His books include Made-Up Interviews with Imaginary Artists (Ugly Duckling Presse, 2009) - a genre-blurring collection of interviews, interview fictions and essays on the art of the interview - and Weird Emptiness: Essays and Aphorisms (Wings Press, 2007). He lives in Boulder and works at the University of Colorado.

books.title: The Artist as Mystic: Conversations with Yahia Lababidi

lababidi-yahia.name: Lababidi, Yahia
lababidi-yahia.bio: Yahia Lababidi is an Egyptian-American poet, essayist and aphorist, the author of some sixteen books of poetry and prose. His first collection of aphorisms, Signposts to Elsewhere, was named a 2008 Book of the Year by The Independent (UK), and his work appears in World Literature Today, AGNI and Philosophy Now, as well as in Geary's Guide to the World's Great Aphorists. In 2012 he served as a juror for the Neustadt Prize, one of the most prestigious international literary awards.

books.title: The Artist as Mystic: Conversations with Yahia Lababidi

pickthall-marmaduke.name: Pickthall, Marmaduke
pickthall-marmaduke.bio: Marmaduke Pickthall (1875-1936) was an English novelist, journalist and traveller, later celebrated for his translation The Meaning of the Glorious Koran (1930). Born in Suffolk, he travelled extensively in the Near East as a young man and converted to Islam in 1917. His fiction and memoirs drew on a deep sympathy for Arab and Ottoman life.

ramuz-charles-ferdinand.name: Ramuz, Charles Ferdinand
ramuz-charles-ferdinand.bio: Charles-Ferdinand Ramuz (1878-1947) was a French-language Swiss novelist and poet, born in Lausanne, in the canton of Vaud. Writing in a distinctive, incantatory prose rooted in the landscape and peasantry of French-speaking Switzerland, he became the central figure of Suisse romande literature; his portrait later appeared on the Swiss 200-franc banknote, and his Histoire du soldat (1918) was written in collaboration with Igor Stravinsky.

books.title: The Reign of the Evil One
Derborence: Where the devils came down

bailat-jones-michelle.name: Bailat-Jones, Michelle
bailat-jones-michelle.bio: Michelle Bailat-Jones is a writer and translator. Born in Japan and raised in the Pacific Northwest, she lives in Switzerland, of which she is now a citizen, and holds an MFA from Emerson College. Her debut novel Fog Island Mountains won the 2013 Christopher Doheny Award from the Center for Fiction; her second, Unfurled, appeared in 2018. She is Translations Editor at Necessary Fiction, and beyond her two Ramuz novels for Skomlin she has translated Claude Cahun and, for Bloomsbury, Corinne Chaponniere's biography of Red Cross founder Henry Dunant.

trueblood-valerie.name: Trueblood, Valerie
trueblood-valerie.bio: Valerie Trueblood is an American novelist and short story writer. She grew up in Virginia, graduated from Brown University, and lives in Seattle. Her first book, Seven Loves (Little, Brown, 2006), a novel told in linked stories, was a Barnes and Noble Discover Great New Writers selection. She has since published the story collections Marry or Burn (2010), a finalist for the Frank O'Connor International Short Story Award; Search Party: Stories of Rescue (2013), a finalist for the 2014 PEN/Faulkner Award; Criminals: Love Stories (2016); and Terrarium: New and Selected Stories (2018), all with Counterpoint. Her short fiction has appeared in magazines including Narrative. She wrote the foreword to Ramuz's Beauty on Earth.

whitall-james.name: Whitall, James
whitall-james.bio: James Whitall (b. 1888) was an American writer and translator, author of the memoir English Years (1935) and translator of Chinese Lyrics from the Book of Jade (1918) and Pierre Hamp's People. His 1922 translation of The Reign of the Evil One (Harcourt, Brace) was the first of Ramuz's books to appear in English; this edition carries an introduction by the critic Ernest Boyd.

books.title: The Reign of the Evil One

boyd-ernest.name: Boyd, Ernest
boyd-ernest.bio: Ernest Boyd (1887-1946) was an Irish born critic, editor and translator. Born in Dublin, he was taught by a French tutor and at schools in Germany and Switzerland, read several European languages, worked on the Irish Times from 1910 to 1913, and then entered the British consular service, with postings in Baltimore, Barcelona and Copenhagen. His Ireland's Literary Renaissance (1916) was the first full account of the Irish literary revival and remained a standard work. He left the consular service and settled in New York in 1920, writing for the New York Evening Post, advising the publisher Alfred A. Knopf, and editing The Independent, the New Freeman and the American Spectator. He also wrote Guy de Maupassant: A Biographical Study (1926). He contributed the introduction to the Harcourt, Brace edition of Ramuz's The Reign of the Evil One in 1922.

books.title: The Reign of the Evil One

marxsen-patti-m.name: Marxsen, Patti M
marxsen-patti-m.bio: Patti M. Marxsen is an American essayist, biographer and translator whose work has appeared in Asymptote, The French Review and the Women's Review of Books. Her critical biography Jacques Roumain: A Life of Resistance won the 2019 Haitian Studies Association Book Prize, and her essay 'Gateau de Payerne' took the inaugural Geneva Writers' Group Literary Award for Non-Fiction. A devotee of Ramuz during her years in Switzerland, she has translated both his prose-poem Riversong of the Rhone and the novel Passage of the Poet. This bilingual edition carries a foreword by Susan Tiberghien.

tiberghien-susan.name: Tiberghien, Susan
tiberghien-susan.bio: Susan Tiberghien is an American writer who has long lived in Geneva. She took a degree in literature and philosophy and did graduate work at the Universite de Grenoble and at the C. G. Jung Institute in Zurich. Her books include the memoirs Looking for Gold: One Year in Jungian Analysis (1997) and Circling to the Center, on silent prayer, together with two books on writing, One Year to a Writing Life (2007) and Writing Toward Wholeness, which draws on Jung. She founded the Geneva Writers' Group in 1993 and directed it for twenty-five years; she is founding editor of its review, Offshoots: Writing from Geneva. She has taught at the International Women's Writing Guild summer conference since 1990 and is a founding member of the writers' residence at the Chateau de Lavigny. She wrote the foreword to Ramuz's Riversong of the Rhone.

spinney-laura.name: Spinney, Laura
spinney-laura.bio: Laura Spinney is a British science journalist and novelist based in Paris. She is the author of the international bestseller Pale Rider: The Spanish Flu of 1918 and How It Changed the World, translated into more than twenty languages, and of Proto: How One Ancient Language Went Global (2025), as well as two novels, The Doctor and The Quick. Her writing appears in National Geographic, Nature, The Economist and The Guardian.

books.title: Derborence: Where the devils came down

kraszewski-j-zef-ignacy.name: Kraszewski, Józef Ignacy
kraszewski-j-zef-ignacy.bio: Jozef Ignacy Kraszewski (1812-1887) was among the most prolific writers in literary history, author of more than 200 novels alongside plays, poetry and historical studies. A Polish novelist, journalist and political activist, he travelled across pre-partition Poland and much of Europe, and is celebrated above all for his cycle of historical novels. Skomlin also publishes Kraszewski's Count Bruhl.

de-savoy-carignan-guy-jean-raoul-euge.name: de Savoy-Carignan, Guy Jean Raoul Eugè
de-savoy-carignan-guy-jean-raoul-euge.bio: Guy Jean Raoul Eugene Charles Emmanuel de Savoie-Carignan, Count de Soissons (born 1860), was a translator and writer who put a number of Polish works into English, usually credited as Count S. C. de Soissons. He translated Jozef Ignacy Kraszewski's The Countess Cosel, published by Downey and Co. in London in 1901, and Count Bruhl, both from Kraszewski's Saxon novels about the court of Augustus the Strong, and supplied an introduction to the first of them calling Kraszewski a reformer of Polish literature. He also translated Eliza Orzeszkowa's An Obscure Apostle (1899) and Henryk Sienkiewicz's So Runs the World, and wrote Boston Artists (1894), A Parisian in America and Six Great Princesses (1913).

boxall-george-e.name: Boxall, George E
boxall-george-e.bio: George E. Boxall was an English-born writer and journalist whose History of the Australian Bushrangers (first published 1899) became a standard early account of colonial outlawry. This edition appends The Jerilderie Letter (1879), Ned Kelly's own manifesto, dictated by the outlaw to explain and justify his campaign against the colonial authorities.

books.title: History of Australian Bushrangers: & The Jerilderie Letter

kelly-ned.name: Kelly, Ned
kelly-ned.bio:
Ned Kelly was born in 1854 in Victoria, the eldest son of an Irish convict transported for pig stealing. He grew up poor in the ranges north of Melbourne, in a community of selectors — small farmers — who had little standing against squatters and less trust in the colonial police. His father died when Ned was twelve. By his mid-teens he was already known to police, apprenticed briefly to the bushranger Harry Power, and cycling through charges. A confrontation with Constable Fitzpatrick in 1878 — disputed then, disputed still — sent him and his brother Dan into the bush for good. The Kelly Gang killed 3 policemen at Stringybark Creek, robbed banks at Euroa and Jerilderie, and held a town at gunpoint at Glenrowan. Kelly walked into the troopers' rifles in homemade plate armour and was captured, tried, and hanged in Melbourne on 11 November 1880. He was 25.

During the Jerilderie bank raid in February 1879, Kelly dictated a 7,500-word document to Joe Byrne and demanded it be printed in the local paper. It wasn't — not in his lifetime. The letter is a furious, vernacular indictment of the colonial system: the police who harassed his family, the squatters who held the land, and the courts that served them both. The prose is raw and run-on, built from the rhythms of spoken Irish-Australian English rather than any schoolroom model. Kelly had almost no formal education. What he produced was closer to an oral manifesto than a written text. Scholars have read it as political philosophy, as self-justification, and as literature. It remains one of the most vivid documents the colonial period produced.

books.title: History of Australian Bushrangers: & The Jerilderie Letter

leskov-nikolai.name: Leskov, Nikolai
leskov-nikolai.bio: Nikolai Leskov (1831-1895) was a Russian novelist, short-story writer and journalist, admired by Chekhov and Gorky for his mastery of vernacular Russian and his vivid portraits of provincial and clerical life. Born in Gorokhovo, Oryol Province, he drew on wide travels across Russia; his tale Lady Macbeth of the Mtsensk District later inspired Shostakovich's opera. Skomlin also publishes Leskov's Cross-eyed Lefty and the Steel Flea.

books.title: Lady Macbeth of the Mzinsk District
Cross-eyed Lefty and the Steel Flea

chamot-alfred.name: Chamot, Alfred
chamot-alfred.bio: Alfred Edward Chamot (1854-1934) was an English translator who spent most of his life in Russia. He was an administrator of the Imperial Palace Gardens at Strelna, near St Petersburg, and left Russia with his family in 1918 after the revolution, settling in London, where he translated Russian literature into English. His version of Nikolai Leskov's Lady Macbeth of the Mtsensk District appeared in the collection The Sentry and Other Stories (John Lane, London, 1922), which also carried his translations of On the Edge of the World, The Sentry and The Toupee Artist, with an introduction by Edward Garnett; Knopf reissued it in New York in 1923. His daughter was the art historian and Tate curator Mary Chamot.

books.title: Lady Macbeth of the Mzinsk District

hapgood-isabel.name: Hapgood, Isabel
hapgood-isabel.bio: Isabel Florence Hapgood (1850-1928) was an American translator and journalist. Born in Boston, she studied at Miss Porter's School until 1868 and then taught herself the Romance, Germanic and Slavic languages. Her first translations, of Tolstoy and Gogol, appeared in 1886, and she went on to translate Hugo, Renan, Dostoevsky, Chekhov, Gorky and Bunin. She spent 1887 to 1889 in Russia, where she met Tolstoy, and wrote Russian Rambles (1895) and A Survey of Russian Literature (1902). For twenty-two years she wrote for the New York Evening Post and the Nation. In 1906 she published her Service Book of the Holy Orthodox-Catholic Apostolic Church, still in use in English-language Orthodox worship. Her version of Leskov's tale, titled The Steel Flea, was printed at the Merrymount Press in Boston in 1916.

books.title: Cross-eyed Lefty and the Steel Flea

hesse-hermann.name: Hesse, Hermann
hesse-hermann.bio: Hermann Hesse (1877-1962) was a German-born Swiss novelist, poet and painter, awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1946. Born in Calw, Germany, and later a citizen of Switzerland, he wrote fiction preoccupied with the individual's search for authenticity and spiritual wholeness. His major works - Siddhartha (1922), Steppenwolf, Demian and The Glass Bead Game - drew on Indian and East Asian thought and made him one of the most widely read European authors of the twentieth century. Skomlin also publishes Hesse's The Journey to the East.

rosner-hilda.name: Rosner, Hilda
rosner-hilda.bio: Hilda Rosner was a translator from German who gave English readers much of Hermann Hesse's fiction. Her version of Siddhartha, published by New Directions in New York in 1951, was the first English rendering of a novel Hesse had finished in 1922, and it remained in print for more than seventy years. She also translated Die Morgenlandfahrt of 1932, which appeared in 1956 as The Journey to the East, and Hesse's earlier novel Gertrude. Skomlin uses her texts for both Siddhartha and The Journey to the East.

joyce-james.name: Joyce, James
joyce-james.bio: James Joyce (1882-1941) was an Irish novelist and poet, one of the most influential writers of the twentieth century and author of Ulysses. Born in Dublin, he spent most of his adult life in continental Europe. 'The Dead', the final and longest story of Dubliners (1914), is widely regarded as one of the finest short stories in the English language.

andreyev-leonid.name: Andreyev, Leonid
andreyev-leonid.bio: Leonid Andreyev (1871-1919) was a Russian writer and playwright, a leading figure of the Silver Age whose intense, often bleak work bridged realism and expressionism. Born in Oryol, he won early fame with stories confronting death, fear and social violence; The Seven Who Were Hanged (1908) is his best-known tale.

bernstein-herman.name: Bernstein, Herman
bernstein-herman.bio: Herman Bernstein (1876-1935) was an American journalist, translator and diplomat, born in Vladislavov in the Russian Empire, in what is now Lithuania. He emigrated to the United States in 1893 and from about 1900 wrote for the New York Evening Post, The Nation and The Independent, later reporting from Europe for the New York Times and the New York Herald. In 1914 he founded the Yiddish daily Der Tog, which he edited until 1916. He covered the Russian Revolution and the 1919 Paris Peace Conference, and in The History of a Lie (1921) he set out the case that the Protocols of the Elders of Zion was a forgery, afterwards suing Henry Ford for libel. He was United States Minister to Albania from 1930 to 1933. His translations from Russian include Leonid Andreyev's The Seven Who Were Hanged, published in English in 1909.

balzac-honor-de.name: Balzac, Honoré de
balzac-honor-de.bio: Honore de Balzac (1799-1850) was a French novelist and playwright whose vast Comedie humaine sought to portray every stratum of post-Napoleonic French society. Born in Tours, he was a founder of literary realism. 'At the Sign of the Cat and Racket' (1830) stands at the head of the Comedie humaine.

books.title: At the Sign of the Cat and Racket

bell-clara.name: Bell, Clara
bell-clara.bio: Clara Bell (1834-1927) was an English translator who worked from eight languages. Born Clara Courtenay Poynter in Westminster, she was the daughter of the architect Ambrose Poynter and the sister of the painter Edward Poynter; in 1856 she married the banker Robert Courtenay Bell, with whom she had six children. Schooled in France, she had French and German early and taught herself Danish, Dutch, Italian, Norwegian, Russian and Spanish after she turned forty. She translated Georg Ebers's historical novels, Spitta's life of Bach, Maupassant, Loti, Ibsen, Perez Galdos and Tolstoy's War and Peace (1886), and she worked on the notebooks of Leonardo da Vinci. For George Saintsbury's edition of the Comedie Humaine, published by Dent from 1895, she translated about a dozen volumes of Balzac, among them At the Sign of the Cat and Racket.

books.title: At the Sign of the Cat and Racket

ruding-walt.name: Ruding, Walt
ruding-walt.bio: Walt Ruding was a late-Victorian author about whom little is now recorded. An Evil Motherhood (1895), styled "an impressionist novel", belongs to the decadent writing of the Yellow Nineties, and Ruding died within weeks of its publication.

books.title: An Evil Motherhood: An Impressionist Novel

proust-marcel.name: Proust, Marcel
proust-marcel.bio: Marcel Proust (1871-1922) was a French novelist whose seven-volume In Search of Lost Time is among the supreme achievements of twentieth-century literature. Born in Auteuil, Paris, he devoted his later years almost entirely to the novel. 'Swann in Love', a self-contained section of Swann's Way, traces a consuming, jealous passion in fashionable Paris.

scott-moncrieff-charles-kenneth.name: Scott Moncrieff, Charles Kenneth
scott-moncrieff-charles-kenneth.bio: Charles Kenneth Scott Moncrieff (1889-1930) was a Scottish translator and soldier. Born in Stirlingshire, he was educated at Winchester College and the University of Edinburgh, where he took first-class honours in Anglo-Saxon in 1914. He served with the King's Own Scottish Borderers on the Western Front from 1914 to 1917, was badly wounded in the leg at Arras in April 1917 and was awarded the Military Cross. His Beowulf appeared in 1919 and his Song of Roland soon after; he also translated Stendhal, Pirandello and the letters of Abelard and Heloise. From 1922 until his death from cancer in Rome he rendered Proust's A la recherche du temps perdu as Remembrance of Things Past, a title Proust disliked. Swann in Love is the central section of his Swann's Way (1922).

turgenev-ivan.name: Turgenev, Ivan
turgenev-ivan.bio: Ivan Turgenev (1818-1883) was a Russian novelist, short-story writer and playwright, the first Russian author to win wide fame across Europe. Born in Oryol into a wealthy landowning family, he spent much of his life in France and Germany and counted Flaubert and the Goncourts among his friends. His major works include Fathers and Sons and A Sportsman's Sketches. Skomlin also publishes Turgenev's The Diary of a Superfluous Man.

books.title: The Diary of a Superfluous Man

garnett-constance.name: Garnett, Constance
garnett-constance.bio: Constance Garnett (1861-1946) was an English translator who brought most of the nineteenth-century Russian canon into English for the first time. Born Constance Black in Brighton, she won a scholarship to Newnham College, Cambridge in 1879 and married the literary critic Edward Garnett in 1889; their son David Garnett became a novelist. She learned Russian in the early 1890s from political exiles in London, published her first translation, Goncharov's A Common Story, in 1894, and travelled to Russia that year, where she met Tolstoy. Over some forty years she produced about seventy volumes of Dostoevsky, Chekhov, Gogol, Tolstoy and Turgenev, working on through failing eyesight. Her fifteen-volume Novels of Ivan Turgenev (1894-1899) included the stories Skomlin publishes as King Lear of the Steppes and The Diary of a Superfluous Man.

books.title: The Diary of a Superfluous Man

baroja-p-o.name: Baroja, Pío
baroja-p-o.bio: Pio Baroja (1872-1956) was a Basque-Spanish novelist, a central figure of Spain's 'Generation of '98' whom Hemingway openly admired. Born in San Sebastian, he wrote spare, restless fiction of Spanish life across dozens of novels. The City of the Discreet is set among the schemers and dreamers of Cordoba.

fassett-jacob.name: Fassett, Jacob
fassett-jacob.bio: Jacob S. Fassett, Jr. translated Pio Baroja's The City of the Discreet (La feria de los discretos) from the Spanish for Alfred A. Knopf, which published it in 1917. He also wrote the introduction to that edition, signed J. S. F., Jr. and dated Cambridge, Massachusetts, October 1917, in which he sets out Baroja's career and writes that the novel was chosen for the series mainly for its Spanish atmosphere. Little else is recorded of him.

olivier-jean-michel.name: Olivier, Jean-Michel
olivier-jean-michel.bio: Jean-Michel Olivier (born 1952 in Nyon, Vaud) is a Swiss novelist, journalist and teacher who studied literature at the University of Geneva under Jean Starobinski and Michel Butor. The author of some twenty novels alongside essays and poetry, he won the Prix Interallie in 2010 for L'Amour negre - a rare Swiss recipient of a major French literary prize. Since 2006 he has directed the Poche Suisse collection at Editions L'Age d'Homme.

moscato-laurence.name: Moscato, Laurence
moscato-laurence.bio: Laurence Moscato is a literary translator working from French into English and a retired professor of translation studies. She lives in New York. Her English translation of Jean-Michel Olivier's Prix Dentan-winning L'Enfant secret, published as The Secret Child (Skomlin, 2018) with a preface by the scholar Clorinda Donato, was praised for its deft rendering of the author's lyrical prose.

donato-clorinda.name: Donato, Clorinda
donato-clorinda.bio: Clorinda Donato is an American scholar of French and Italian. She is Professor of Italian and French at California State University, Long Beach, where she holds the George L. Graziadio Chair of Italian Studies and directs the university's centre for global Romance languages and translation studies. Her work covers eighteenth-century encyclopedias and knowledge transfer through translation, gender in medical and literary writing, and intercomprehension across the Romance languages. Her books include The Life and Legend of Catterina Vizzani (2020) and the textbook Juntos: Italian for Speakers of English and Spanish (2020). She was made Chevalier dans l'Ordre des Palmes Academiques in 2005 and received the CSULB Outstanding Professor Award in 2016. For Skomlin she edited and wrote the preface to The Secret Child (2018), Laurence Moscato's translation of Jean-Michel Olivier's L'Enfant secret.

weeks-john.name: Weeks, John
weeks-john.bio: John Weeks studied French, Russian and Polish at Amherst College and holds a doctorate in Slavic languages and literatures from the University of California, Berkeley, where he later taught Polish following a Fulbright fellowship in Poland. He has translated widely from Russian and Polish; Farinet's Gold is his first published literary translation.

mann-thomas.name: Mann, Thomas
mann-thomas.bio: Thomas Mann (1875-1955) was a German novelist and Nobel laureate (1929), author of Buddenbrooks, The Magic Mountain and Death in Venice. Born in Lubeck, he went into exile after 1933 in opposition to Nazism. Royal Highness (1909), his second novel, is a gently ironic romance set in a minor German principality.

dos-passos-john.name: Dos Passos, John
dos-passos-john.bio: John Dos Passos (1896-1970) was an American novelist and one of the foremost chroniclers of the modern age, best known for his U.S.A. trilogy. Born in Chicago, he served as a volunteer ambulance driver in the First World War and travelled widely in Europe. Skomlin also publishes Dos Passos's One Man's Initiation: 1917.

reymont-wladyslaw-stanislaw.name: Reymont, Wladyslaw Stanislaw
reymont-wladyslaw-stanislaw.bio: Wladyslaw Reymont (1867-1925) was a Polish novelist and Nobel laureate (1924), best known for his four-volume epic The Peasants. Born near Kobiele Wielkie, he worked as an actor and a railway official before turning to writing. The Comedienne (1896) draws on his own experience of the provincial theatre.

obecny-edmund.name: Obecny, Edmund
obecny-edmund.bio: Edmund Obecny made the first English translation of Wladyslaw Stanislaw Reymont's novel The Comedienne (Komediantka), published by G. P. Putnam's Sons in New York and London in 1920 under the Knickerbocker Press imprint, four years before Reymont won the Nobel Prize in Literature. The novel follows a young provincial woman who leaves home to join a travelling theatre company. The 1920 edition opens with an unsigned publishers' note rather than a translator's preface, and nothing further is recorded of Obecny beyond this translation.

rolland-romain.name: Rolland, Romain
rolland-romain.bio: Romain Rolland (1866-1944) was a French novelist, dramatist and Nobel laureate (1915), a committed pacifist best known for the ten-volume Jean-Christophe. Born in Clamecy, he wrote Pierre and Luce during the First World War as a protest against its slaughter.

de-kay-charles.name: de Kay, Charles
de-kay-charles.bio: Charles de Kay (1848-1935) was an American writer, critic and diplomat. Born in Washington, D.C., the son of the naval officer George Coleman de Kay, he graduated from Yale in 1868 and spent eighteen years, from 1876 to 1894, as literary and art critic of the New York Times. He helped found the Authors Club, the National Sculpture Society, the Fencers Club and, in 1898, the National Arts Club. He published poetry and prose under his own name and the pen names Henry Eckford and Louis Barnaval, among them The Bohemian (1878), Hesperus (1880) and Bird Gods (1898), and he wrote on the sculptor Antoine-Louis Barye and on Louis Comfort Tiffany. From 1894 he was United States consul general in Berlin. He translated Romain Rolland's Pierre and Luce, published by Henry Holt in 1922.

barbusse-henri.name: Barbusse, Henri
barbusse-henri.bio: Henri Barbusse (1873-1935) was a French novelist and journalist, best known for Under Fire (Le Feu, 1916), his searing novel of the trenches which won the Prix Goncourt. Born in Asnieres-sur-Seine, he was a committed pacifist and, later, a communist. Hell (L'Enfer, 1908) preceded his war writing.

o-brien-edward-j.name: O'Brien, Edward J.
o-brien-edward-j.bio: Edward J. O'Brien (1890-1941) was an American anthologist, editor, poet and translator. Born in Boston, he spent a year at Harvard and in 1915 began The Best Short Stories, the annual selection of American short fiction he edited until his death and which Martha Foley then carried on. He moved to Europe in 1919 and settled in England, where he also edited yearbooks of British short stories and wrote The Dance of the Machines (1929), on the American short story and industrial life, and Son of the Morning (1932), a portrait of Nietzsche. He was married to the English novelist Romer Wilson from 1923 until her death in 1932, and in his last years he was European story editor for MGM's British studios. His translation of Henri Barbusse's Hell appeared in 1918 as The Inferno, with an introduction of his own.
